items.title: What are ‘civilian’ sites in international law and where have US, Iran hit?
items.summary: The US has escalated attacks on Iranian roads, bridges and power plants, and Iran too, has responded.

scraped.title: What are ‘civilian’ sites in international law and where have US, Iran hit?
scraped.description: The US has escalated attacks on Iranian roads, bridges and power plants, and Iran too, has responded.
scraped.author: Shola Lawal
scraped.h1: What are ‘civilian’ sites in international law and where have US, Iran hit?
scraped.body_text:
The United States has escalated attacks on Iranian roads, bridges and power plants, and Iran too, has responded.

Save

Share

The United States and Iran are locked in an increasingly escalatory cycle of strikes that they each claim is aimed at preventing the other from securing military dominance over the Strait of Hormuz.

As the US pounds southern Iran and, in recent days, other parts of the country, Tehran too has hit back, striking US military bases in neighbouring nations in the Gulf and Jordan.

But projectiles fired by both the US and Iran have also hit civilian infrastructure, raising questions over potential violations of international law, even as the fragile memorandum of understanding (MoU) towards peace that the two countries had signed in June has collapsed.

“We’re going to knock out all their power plants. We’re going to knock out all their bridges unless they get to the table and negotiate,” US President Donald Trump threatened in a Fox News interview last week. He made similar threats on civilian infrastructure earlier in April.

At least 50 people have died in Iran since the resumption of hostilities, and 500 have been wounded since July 15, according to Iranian authorities. Dozens of locations in southern and northwestern Iran have been hit in the past week, ranging from military command centres to railways and airports.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has hit back on neighbouring Gulf countries hosting US military assets, resulting in the deaths of at least two US military personnel.

International humanitarian law explicitly forbids the targeting of civilian infrastructure in armed conflict. The US and Israel hit several civilian sites in the first phase of the war that they launched against Iran on February 28, including a girls’ school in Minab where at least 170 people were killed.

A spokesperson for United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Friday that he was “particularly concerned about attacks on civilian infrastructure in Iran and across the region”, adding that “such attacks are unacceptable”.

So what counts as civilian infrastructure, and what places have been hit so far in the second wave of the US-Israel war on Iran? Here’s what we know:

The 1949 Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols of 1977 forbid armed attacks or reprisals on civilian infrastructure or “objects” during a conflict.

Civilian infrastructure includes “all objects which are not military objectives”, the law says, and which are “normally dedicated to civilian purposes, such as a place of worship, a house, or other dwelling or a school”.

These also include any facilities that support the day-to-day lives of civilians and that are crucial to how a society functions: roads, bridges, railways, airports, electrical plants, sewage systems, hospitals, and phone and internet systems, for example.

The treaty states that drinking water installations and supplies, irrigation works, foodstuffs, crops, livestock as well as dams, dikes, and nuclear power generation plants also cannot be targeted.

When in doubt about whether an object is serving a military or civilian purpose, parties must assume it is civilian and thus cannot attack it, the law states.

Yes, under specific and carefully determined circumstances.

Civilian infrastructure becomes a legitimate target only when it can be proven that it was “used for military purposes at the time of the attack and that its destruction provides a definite military advantage”, according to the treaty.

Even so, the law mandates that such attacks ensure that necessary attacks on civilian infrastructure remain “proportionate to the military advantage”.

In short, attacks on suspected civilian objects are prohibited if the risks to civilians – deaths, injury, and the proper functioning of civilian life – outweigh military gains.

“The basic presumption is that infrastructure is civilian and protected until such time it has become a military objective through the enemy’s use or future use,” Luke Moffett, law professor and civilian harm expert at Queen’s University Belfast, told Al Jazeera.

The US and NATO forces used this justification for past attacks on electrical or water plants in Iraq or Libya, although they caused civilian harm, the professor said.

Because there’s such a thin line between preventing the enemy from using infrastructure and impacting civilians, militaries have to constantly verify that targets provide a military advantage and that civilian harm is not excessive, he added.

“Otherwise it can be an indiscriminate attack,” Moffett said. Such indiscriminate attacks can be prosecuted as war crimes.

Iranian media and officials have reported several US strikes on civilian infrastructure as defined by the Geneva treaty, particularly in southern coastline areas close to the Strait of Hormuz. Washington claims it has exclusively targeted “including military logistics infrastructure”.

Analysts say lawyers in the US military may be clearing some targets for strikes as “dual-use”, meaning they might potentially be used for military purposes.

Road and bridge networks

Health facilities

Water and food facilities

Airports and seaports

Communication towers

Residential areas, sewage systems and administrative buildings

Nuclear power plants

Iran has repeatedly targeted military bases – and increasingly, civilian infrastructure – in Kuwait, Oman, Jordan and Qatar. The IRGC insists it is targeting US military assets.

items.title: What we know about US soldiers killed in Iran war, and Iranian casualties
items.summary: Trump has expressed sadness and vowed to hit Iran 'very hard' to honour killed US soldiers.

scraped.title: What we know about US soldiers killed in Iran war, and Iranian casualties
scraped.description: Trump has expressed sadness and vowed to hit Iran ‘very hard’ to honour killed US soldiers.
scraped.author: Sarah Shamim
scraped.h1: What we know about US soldiers killed in Iran war, and Iranian casualties
scraped.body_text:
Trump has expressed sadness and vowed to hit Iran ‘very hard’ to honour killed US soldiers.

Save

Share

Trump: Latest strikes on Iran 'in honour' of killed US military personnel

The United States military said on Sunday that a US service member was killed on Saturday in northern Iraq, where US forces are based.

The US Central Command (CENTCOM), which is responsible for operations in the Middle East, said the soldier died during a controlled detonation of what it called unexploded ordnance on a downed Iranian attack drone.

How many US soldiers died in the Iran war?

The latest casualty announcements increased to 17 the number of US military personnel killed since the war began, and at least 420 wounded — with at least one missing.

The war began on February 28, when the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran and the Iranians retaliated, hitting US military assets in the Gulf.

Before the US and Iran signed their memorandum of understanding (MoU) on June 17 to extend their ceasefire and continue peace talks, the US military confirmed 13 combat-related deaths across the region. They included six crew when a US refuelling aircraft crashed in western Iraq in early March.

Additionally, one service member died of a “health-related incident” in Kuwait.

The MoU triggered a 60-day negotiation period. While ceasefire negotiations remained precarious, hostilities largely subsided until July 7, when the latest crossfire began.

The US and Iran have traded attacks since then. On Sunday night, the US announced it had concluded its ninth consecutive night of attacks against Iran. Iran hit back with ballistic missiles hitting US transport planes at Aqaba airport in Jordan.

The US military said earlier on Sunday that two service personnel died in Jordan and a third was missing in action.

Also on Sunday, CENTCOM said that “unidentified remains” had been found at the site of Friday’s attack and that “an examination process to verify the remains is ongoing”.

While the US has not officially released the names of all 17 of the personnel killed in the Iran war, the US defence department on Monday released the names of two of them.

Tyler James Feehan, 25, was killed on Saturday and Isabella Gonzales, 19, died on Friday during an attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. The “incident” is under investigation, the military said.

On March 14, the Department released the names of six air force personnel who were killed during the refuelling incident in Iraq two days earlier: John Klinner, 33; Ariana Savino, 31; Ashley Pruitt, 34; Seth Koval, 38; Curtis Angst, 30; and Tyler Simmons, 28.

On March 3, the department announced that Cody Khork, 35; Noah Tietjens, 42; Nicole Amor, 39; and Declan Coady, 20, died on March 1, 2026, in Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, during an unmanned aircraft system attack. On March 4, it announced that Jeffrey O’Brien, 45, also died on March 1 in Port Shuaiba. On March 11, the Department said army reserve soldier Robert Marzan, 54, died during the same attack.

Benjamin Pennington, 26, died on March 8 of injuries sustained on March 1 during an attack at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia

President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the deaths of the US soldiers in the Iranian attack on Jordan on Friday were “a very sad thing”.

“We’re never allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he added.

Trump said later that the US is hitting Iran “very hard” to honour service members who have been killed.

“We hit them very hard again tonight,” Trump told reporters as he returned to Washington from the World Cup final.

A poll conducted by Reuters and Ipsos late last month found that only about one in four Americans believed Trump’s war with Iran was worth its costs.

Most respondents expressed concern about the economic and security fallout.

On January 28, 2024, three US soldiers were killed and more than 40 wounded in a drone attack on the ‘Tower 22’ site on the Jordanian–Syrian border.

On November 4, 2016, three US soldiers from the 5th Special Forces Group were killed and another wounded when Jordanian Sergeant Maarek Sami Abu Tayeh opened fire on them as they were entering King Faisal Air Base in Jordan. They had been working as part of a programme to train Syrian fighters under US supervision.

On November 9, 2015, when a Jordanian officer opened fire inside the King Abdullah II Special Operations Training Center, killing five people: two American contractors working in security training programmes, two South African security personnel, and a Jordanian trainer. Jordanian security forces responded and killed the attacker.

The death toll in the Iran war is a fraction of the thousands killed in the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Seventeen soldiers have been killed in the Iran war, which has spanned 142 days.

In the Iraq war spanning 3,195 days from 2003 to 2011, more than 4,400 US military personnel were killed.

In the Afghanistan war, which lasted 7,267 days from 2001 to 2021, more than 2,400 US military personnel were killed.

The US death toll in the Iran war is still relatively low, though higher than in previous air campaigns, such as Kosovo and Libya.

In the 1999 Kosovo air campaign, which lasted 78 days, and the 2011 Libya air campaign, which lasted 227 days, the US recorded very few or no combat fatalities from enemy fire. Accidents were the biggest risk.

The overall death tolls were in single digits or low double digits.

On July 18, Iran’s Health Ministry reported that at least 50 people were killed and at least 500 injured in US strikes in July.

From when the war started until the MoU was reached in June, at least 3,468 people were killed in US-Israeli attacks on Iran. They were aged between eight months and 88 years and included seven infants, 376 older children and 496 women.

During that time, more than 26,500 people were injured, including at least 4,000 women and 1,621 children.

Several key members of the Iranian leadership have been killed during the war, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, senior security chief Ali Larijani, the Basij paramilitary commander Gholamreza Soleimani and several other senior Iranian commanders.

items.summary: The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.

scraped.title: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
scraped.description: The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.
scraped.h1: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
scraped.body_text:
The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.

Russia said Monday that a Ukrainian strike on a bus in the border region of Belgorod killed five civilians, including a minor, and left three others critically injured.

The attack came after a Ukrainian retaliatory strike on Moscow, with city officials reporting that more than 400 drones targeted the Russian capital.

The latest escalation followed Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities over the weekend.

In eastern Ukraine , Russian attacks on Pavlograd and Kramatorsk killed two people in each city, according to local authorities.

Officials also reported one person killed in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia during Russian bombardment.

Both sides have previously denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine targeted the Russian capital with more than 400 drones from Sunday into Monday, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

He added that most of the drones were intercepted, but Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said at least 10 people were wounded by Ukrainian drones.

Several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were also damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces were targeting Russian logistics facilities and an oil depot in the region.

"We are responding, justly, to every Russian strike against our cities and communities," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military publicly denied rumors that Zelenskyy was firing the chief of Ukraine's armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy has faced criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

There have been days of protests in Ukraine following Fedorov's removal, as a long-running dispute between the reform-minded minister and Syrskyi spilled into the open.

Zelenskyy appointed Yevhenii Khmara, the acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as acting defense minister and asked parliament to approve him for the position.

On Monday, he posted several messages on social media showing him meeting with Ukraine's top military commanders to discuss the latest developments in the war, which has dragged on for more than four years.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

items.title: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
items.summary: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?

scraped.title: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
scraped.description: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?
scraped.h1: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
scraped.body_text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?

Monday marks the 52nd anniversary of Turkey's 1974 invasion of Cyprus , which led to the division of the island.

Five decades later, the Cyprus issue remains one of the world's longest-running unresolved disputes.

The United Nations announced last week that Antonio Guterres is due to visit Cyprus from July 27 to 29 — the first visit by a UN secretary-general in 16 years — in an effort to breathe new life into the stalled peace process.

His visit marks the culmination of a renewed UN initiative that was launched after an informal enlarged meeting on Cyprus held in Geneva in March.

Since then, the UN secretary-general's personal envoy, Maria Angela Holguin, has held a series of consultations in Cyprus, Greece, Turkey , the United Kingdom and Brussels to assess whether the political conditions exist for meaningful negotiations to resume.

During his stay in Cyprus, Guterres will hold separate meetings with President of the Republic of Cyprus Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman.

On July 29, the two leaders are expected to meet jointly with the UN chief at the residence of the UN Special Representative in the UN-controlled buffer zone.

The last time a UN secretary-general visited Cyprus was in 2010, when Ban Ki-moon sought to inject political momentum into negotiations between then President of the Republic of Cyprus Demetris Christofias and Turkish Cypriot leader Mehmet Ali Talat.

Both leaders came from left-wing political parties that supported a bizonal, bicommunal federation and were widely seen as having the political will to pursue a comprehensive settlement.

That momentum, however, faded only months later after Talat lost the Turkish Cypriot leadership election to Dervis Eroglu, while major disagreements over the core chapters of the negotiations remained unresolved.

Ban's efforts were preceded by the intensive engagement of Kofi Annan between 2002 and 2004, when the UN undertook its most ambitious effort to broker a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue.

Annan became personally involved in the negotiations, presenting a series of revised versions of what became known as the Annan Plan.

The initiative culminated in simultaneous referendums in April 2004. The proposal was approved by a majority of Turkish Cypriot voters but rejected by 75.8% of Greek Cypriot voters.

Guterres' visit comes amid reports that the UN is exploring a possible new framework for resolving the Cyprus issue.

The discussion gained momentum after Britain's The Independent reported on July 12 that Holguin is working on a revised settlement proposal.

According to the newspaper, the framework would retain the agreed model of a bizonal, bicommunal federation, as set out in relevant UN Security Council resolutions, while granting significantly greater autonomy to the two constituent states and limiting the powers of the federal government.

The report also claims that, in exchange for this broader autonomy, the Turkish Cypriot side would be expected to accept territorial adjustments, including the return of the fenced-off city of Varosha and the town of Morphou.

It also suggests that new security arrangements are being considered that would allow Greek and Turkish troops to remain on the island under NATO command.

According to The Independent , the proposal seeks to bridge the gap between the Greek Cypriot commitment to a federal settlement and Turkey's long-standing support for a two-state solution.

The UN has neither confirmed nor denied the report.

Asked about it, President Christodoulides said that "not everything reported by the newspaper is accurate," adding that he expects further developments in the coming period.

Despite the expectations surrounding Guterres' visit, diplomats say the UN chief's immediate objective is not to discuss a draft settlement plan.

Diplomatic sources who spoke to DW believe the most likely outcome of the meetings next week will be the announcement of a new informal expanded meeting bringing together the leaders of Cyprus' two communities, representatives of Greece, Turkey and the UK — the island's three guarantor powers under the 1960 treaties — and the UN.

According to the same sources, such a meeting could take place in late August or early September. Unlike previous informal gatherings, however, the UN is said to be seeking a more structured process this time, with a clearer sequence of steps and a defined timeframe.

Although Guterres' renewed engagement is inevitably linked to the final months of his second term, which ends in December, diplomatic sources believe the latest initiative is driven by more than his limited remaining time in office.

For the first time in years, they believe conditions for a renewed political dialogue may be emerging.

A key factor has been the election of Tufan Erhurman as Turkish Cypriot leader last October . Unlike his predecessor, Ersin Tatar, who advocated a two-state solution, Erhurman has said he is prepared to resume negotiations on the basis of a bizonal, bicommunal federation.

That change does not represent a shift in Turkey's official policy, nor does it resolve longstanding disagreements over security, guarantees, political equality or the continued presence of Turkish troops on the island.

It has, however, created conditions that allow the UN to test whether a meaningful return to negotiations is now possible.

Cyprus government spokesperson Konstantinos Letymbiotis believes Guterres' visit should also be viewed in the context of a broader increase in international diplomatic activity on Cyprus.

"The secretary-general's initiative, the European Union 's stronger engagement and the appointment of Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's envoy on Cyprus are creating new momentum," he told DW.

On July 8, European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen discussed the UN initiative with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, urging Ankara to make use of the renewed diplomatic momentum on Cyprus.

A few days later, the Commission appointed Raffaele Fitto as its special representative for the Cyprus issue.

The move was widely interpreted as a sign that Brussels intends to play a more substantive role in the process, while underlining that any future settlement must be fully compatible with EU law.

The EU's increased involvement is also closely linked to the broader trajectory of EU-Turkey relations.

From Brussels' perspective, progress on the Cyprus issue could facilitate movement on several key areas of cooperation with Ankara.

Conversely, the absence of progress continues to be one of the main obstacles preventing any meaningful upgrade in relations between the EU and Turkey.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

items.title: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
items.summary: A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?

scraped.title: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
scraped.description: A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?
scraped.h1: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
scraped.body_text:
A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?

Now more than four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , the Black Sea has become one of Europe's key security frontiers. And yet, it is currently "quite empty of warships," Thomas de Waal, a senior fellow at Carnegie Europe, told DW. This, he said, "is a bit of a paradox." To understand that paradox, we first need to need to take a closer look at the map.

The Black Sea is bordered by six countries: Turkey , Bulgaria , Romania , Ukraine , Russia , and Georgia . The first three on that list are part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO — the other three are not. To make matters more complicated, two of the latter three are at war with each other.

Access to the Black Sea runs through a single, narrow bottleneck. To get there, a ship coming from the Mediterranean Sea would have to pass the Dardanelles Straits and the Bosporus, which crosses through the heart of Turkey's largest metropolis Istanbul .

At its narrowest point, the Bosporus is just 700 meters (0.4 miles) wide. For comparison, another critical passageway currently in the headlines is the Strait of Hormuz , which is approximately 33 kilometers (21 miles) wide at its narrowest point.

It is this geographic bottleneck to the Black Sea that makes it "an economic choke point," said de Waal. "Whoever controls the Turkish Straits also controls, to some extent, trade through the Black Sea and also has an enormous military advantage."

Russia also has a special interest in the Black Sea, according to Daria Isachenko, a visiting fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs. "A strong military position in the Black Sea for Russia is not an end in itself, but also a means to advance its geopolitical ambitions beyond and also strengthen its great power status."

The second part of the equation goes back to a treaty signed exactly 90 years ago.

On July 20, 1936, representatives from just under a dozen countries gathered in the Swiss town of Montreux to settle a long-standing dilemma: How — and by whom — should these vital waterways be governed? They established the Montreux Convention, an agreement that essentially restored Turkey's sovereignty over the Dardanelles Strait and Bosporus. This came after years of international oversight, following the Ottoman Empire's defeat in the First World War .

Negotiations resulted in a document of nearly 30 pages, which set the legal framework that governs the Turkish Straits to this day. The treaty keeps the straits open to passenger and commercial traffic during peacetime — crucial for the important trade route.

When it comes to military ships, Black Sea states are allowed to move their warships through the straits relatively freely. Any navy from outside the region faces restrictions on their fleet size, tonnage, and how long they are allowed to stay in the sea — no longer than 21 days during peacetime.

During times of war, these rules become stricter. When Turkey is not part of the conflict, warships belonging to any nation involved in the fight are not allowed to pass through — a clause that has had profound consequences for the region since February 2022.

This special system of access rights keeps the Turkish government in a very powerful position. "The most privileged Black Sea state is Türkiye itself," Isachenko said.

It also helps explain why NATO doesn't maintain a continuous presence in the Black Sea — unlike in other waters such as the Mediterranean or the North Sea. "For NATO, Montreux is a constraint," Isachenko pointed out. "For Türkiye, it is an instrument to keep the balance in the Black Sea."

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in late February 2022, the Montreux Convention arguably faced its greatest test in decades. A few days after the military operation began, Turkey invoked Article 19 of the treaty, which applies during wartime and restricts military ships belonging to countries engaged in the fight from passing through the straits.

Essentially, from that point onwards, neither Russia, nor Ukraine, could freely reinforce their naval forces in the Black Sea — with one exception: warships registered to a home port in the Black Sea could return to their base.

"I think the Montreux Convention and Turkey's policy at the beginning of the war was absolutely crucial in allowing Ukraine to survive," Thomas de Waal told DW.

He argued that it prevented Russia from adding more vessels to their Black Sea fleet, saying that "up to 30 Russian ships stayed outside." This, he added, contributed to Ukraine holding "the upper hand in the Black Sea."

Those restrictions may also have highlighted how warfare itself has changed, with Ukraine turning to drones and other modern technology not covered by the 1936 document. "Ukraine didn't build military vessels," according to Iulian Chifu, a Romanian foreign policy analyst. "It just shifted the generation of attack," he said.

The maritime treaty has also restricted the options available to Ukraine's supporters in the West. In 2024, the United Kingdom donated two minesweepers to Ukraine, which were unable to enter the Black Sea, according to the UK Ministry of Defence. That's because Turkey considers them to be "vessels of war," according to de Waal. Instead, the ships have been docked in Portsmouth, in southern England.

For de Waal, this illustrates Turkey's wider approach: "It's a very carefully constructed strategy," he said," in which Turkey basically says to other NATO countries: 'Leave us alone in the Black Sea, we will handle this.'"

Key to the convention's enduring relevance may be its long-standing recognition by states. "Turkey has come up with an arrangement, a regime, which Russia is not especially happy about, but accepts, and that's very important," he noted.

At a time when the international rules-based order has increasingly come under pressure , the Montreux Convention stands out as a rare example of a multilateral diplomatic mechanism that is still observed and respected 90 years after it was signed.

The geography of the Turkish Straits — plus their complex governance structure — have led to NATO rethinking how it can operate in the region. At times, the issue even creates some tension between its alliance members: "In the Black Sea," de Waal explained, "Turkey is very much Turkey first and NATO second."

This security logic, he argued, has shaped Turkey's message to its Western allies: "We don't want to see your permanent presence in the Black Sea, but Romania and Bulgaria have this shared Black Sea ownership, so you can support them."

As a result, greater focus has been placed on these two Eastern European states, which have been NATO members since 2004. However, some experts remain doubtful: "The military capabilities of Bulgaria and Romania," said Chifu, "are barely limited to their capacity of defending their territories."

Nevertheless, he argued that Romania had been "trying to improve our capabilities building ships," as well as purchasing military assets, with the aim of "enforcing our footprint in the Black Sea."

One example is the planned expansion of Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near the Romanian port city Constanța. Romania's government is expected to spend € 2.5 billion ($ 2.8 billion) on transforming it into the largest NATO military base in Europe — bigger than Ramstein, a US military base in Germany.

Earlier this month, the region was in the spotlight once again, as leaders of NATO's member states met in the Turkish capital Ankara for their annual summit . There, Turkey, Romania, and Bulgaria announced a trilateral task group for mine-clearing efforts to protect underwater infrastructure.

The Montreux Convention is "quite an archaic document," de Waal told DW, pointing out that it still refers to the League of Nations — the UN 's predecessor, which ceased to exist 80 years ago. "But I think no one wants to touch it," out of concern that it "opens a kind of Pandora's box when all the issues have to be renegotiated with Russia," he added.

"For Türkiye," said Isachenko, Montreux "also belongs to a number of founding treaties of the Turkish Republic." Beyond its role as a maritime access treaty, it reflects Turkey's core interests: "sovereignty, security and status," she added, so challenging Montreux means "dealing, revising and challenging" those core interests.

Security analyst Chifu stressed that he was "not revisionist" and believed the convention should stay in place while the Ukraine war rages on. "But after the war," he said, "we should reconsider very clearly how this is applied to our allies in NATO."

To him, the question of how exactly the treaty's clauses are applied and interpreted by Turkey remains a sore point.

"You have no option but to work with Turkey," is the key message de Waal took away from the recent NATO summit in Ankara. "You can't work without it," he said, referring to what he calls the strongest power in the Black Sea.

For the past nine decades, the Montreux Convention has outlasted wars, leaders, and entire generations. And as long as it lasts, Turkey holds sway over the Black Sea gateway.

items.summary: The United States conducted a new round of airstrikes early Monday targeting Iran after announcing the death of another service member. Iran responded by launching an attack targeting Bahrain, the home of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, as well as Kuwait.

scraped.title: U.S identifies 2 soldiers killed in Jordan as it exchanges strikes with Iran | CBC News
scraped.description: The United States conducted a new round of airstrikes early Monday targeting Iran after announcing the death of another service member. Iran responded by launching an attack targeting Bahrain, the home of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, as well as Kuwait.
scraped.h1: U.S identifies 2 soldiers killed in Jordan as it exchanges strikes with Iran
scraped.body_text:
The United States conducted a new round of airstrikes early Monday targeting Iran after announcing the death of another service member. Iran responded by launching an attack targeting Bahrain, the home of the U.S. navy's 5th Fleet, and Kuwait.

Both sides in recent days have targeted civilian infrastructure relied on by millions of people, while benchmark Brent crude rose Monday above $90 US a barrel, further fuelling a global energy crisis sparked by the conflict.

The latest attacks showed how the U.S. and Iran have inched closer to all-out war again after a pause last month — when both sides reached a memorandum of understanding and were working toward a permanent end to the fighting and restoring shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to pre-war levels.

The U.S. military's Central Command announced a new round of strikes early Monday, now into their ninth straight night. Central Command said it targeted "Iranian military command centres, air defence and coastal surveillance sites, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites and communications networks."

"We hit them very hard again tonight," U.S. President Donald Trump said separately, adding the U.S. did it in honour of its recently killed service members.

Trump has also threatened to target Iran's power stations and bridges to try to compel Tehran to loosen its hold on the Strait of Hormuz, which saw one-fifth of traded global oil supplies transit before the war.

Since Friday, three. U.S. service members have been killed. The Defence Department in a statement on Monday identified 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas, as having been killed in Jordan, where they were supporting a U.S. mission against the Islamic State.

It's unclear how they were killed, but Central Command had previously reported two deaths in Jordan amid Iranian missile and drone attacks.

A third death was announced on Sunday, of a U.S. service member who was in Iraq.

U.S. military deaths prompt fears of a wider war with Iran

The U.S. military has said 17 of its troops have died since it launched, with Israel, the war against Iran on Feb. 28.

The deaths reflect the complicated reality that American soldiers don't need to be on the ground in Iran for there to be lethal risks in a conflict that involves drones, missiles and airplanes. American forces are arrayed across the Middle East, making other nations targets of Iran as the fighting has escalated.

Iran's state-run IRNA news agency reported Monday that the American strikes killed at least one person around Tabriz, a northwestern city about 520 kilometres from the capital, Tehran. Tabriz is believed to host underground missile bases run by Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard.

U.S. strikes likely also hit Bandar Imam Khomeini in Khuzestan province, Sirik and Jask in Hormozgan province and Konarak and Chahbahar in Sistan and Baluchistan province, IRNA reported.

As the latest round of strikes began, a vessel caught fire early Monday in the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by a projectile near the coastline of Oman, the British military's United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said. The crew abandoned the vessel, which was adrift and still ablaze hours later, the centre said.

The route around Oman has been the one the U.S. military has encouraged ships to travel to avoid Iran's control. The Guard later claimed it was targeting tankers in the strait.

Iran supreme leader threatens to teach U.S. 'unforgettable lessons' if attacks continue

The U.S. in the past week reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports to halt its shipments of crude oil.

Iranian authorities on Sunday said at least 50 people have been killed and 517 wounded in the latest rounds of U.S. strikes.

items.title: Dozens feared dead after passenger ferry sinks off coast of Guyana
items.summary: No survivors have been found ‌since Sunday afternoon, when Guyanese authorities announced they had rescued 67 people, including 15 children.

scraped.title: Dozens feared dead after passenger ferry sinks off coast of Guyana | CBC News
scraped.description: No survivors have been found ‌since Sunday afternoon, when Guyanese authorities announced they had rescued 67 people, including 15 children.
scraped.h1: Dozens feared dead after passenger ferry sinks off coast of Guyana
scraped.body_text:
Dozens of people were feared dead after a ferry carrying as many as 133 people capsized off the coast of Guyana late on Saturday, with authorities suggesting an inaccurate passenger list and drug use by the crew might have contributed to the situation.

No survivors have been found ‌since Sunday afternoon, when Guyanese authorities announced they had rescued 67 people, including 15 children.

The captain and other crew members are now in police custody, Public Works Minister Juan Edghill said at a news conference late on Sunday.

"Search and rescue is still in progress," Edghill said. "So to the families that are out there wondering about their loved ones, we ​are doing everything that is humanly possible to find them."

The MV Barima, which ​had 116 passengers and 17 crew members, capsized off the North Atlantic coast, approximately 11 kilometres from shore, while travelling from the capital Georgetown to the village of Port Kaituma, authorities said.

Air traffic control received a ​distress call from the ferry around 11 p.m. on Saturday, triggering a search and rescue operation.

Edghill said early ⁠responses were hampered by the ⁠darkness and lack of vessels with scanners that could search for survivors, ‌leaving rescuers reliant on eyesight and sound.

Companies in the oil and gas sector have since deployed vessels with scanners and the government has activated divers to enter the ferry to search for bodies, Edghill said. Authorities have also expanded the search area to 1,040 square kilometres, up from 400 square kilometres.

Edghill initially insisted on Sunday afternoon ⁠that there was no sign of "neglect" on the part of the ferry operator. But on Sunday evening, he said the captain and at least one other crew members had tested positive for marijuana.

In addition, a number of people who were rescued were not listed on the ferry's manifest, ‌indicating inaccuracies in the ferry's passenger list and hampering rescue operations because authorities do not know how many people they are searching for.

The boat had maintenance in 2024 and was due for dry docking — the process of temporarily taking a ship out of water to inspect and repair problems — later this year, the minister said.

The disaster has torn apart ​families.

Leon Murray, a passenger on the ferry, told local news outlet Ignite News that about four hours after leaving Georgetown, someone shouted that the boat was sinking.

After the boat ⁠capsized, Murray managed to swim to the surface where he used a life jacket to keep himself afloat. He drifted and shouted ⁠for help and found his son and three others holding on to a floating box.

Murray said he and his son survived, ⁠but ⁠his wife, daughter and four grandchildren haven't been found. "Six ​of them gone."

Guyanese Prime Minister Mark Phillips said in a statement that the vessel reported a cargo weight of 268 tons out ​of a capacity of 284 tons. He ⁠said the ferry was licensed to carry more than 300 passengers, and was outfitted with 250 life jackets, six inflatable life rafts and two rigid life rafts.

But by Sunday evening, at a news conference, Phillips said an investigation had been launched into wrongdoing involving members of the police force, the defence force and the maritime administration department.

"Let me be absolutely clear: where negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing is established, those responsible will face the full force ⁠of the law."

items.title: Andy Burnham officially becomes British prime minister
items.summary: Andy Burnham became the fifth British prime minister in four years and the seventh in a decade as he formally accepted an invitation from King Charles to form a government.

scraped.title: Andy Burnham becomes Britain's 7th PM in past decade | CBC News
scraped.description: Andy Burnham became the fifth British prime minister in four years and the seventh in a decade as he formally accepted an invitation from King Charles to form a government.
scraped.h1: Andy Burnham officially becomes British prime minister
scraped.body_text:
Britain needs to show the world it can regain stability, new PM says

Andy Burnham became the fifth British prime minister in four years and the seventh in a decade as he formally accepted an invitation from King Charles to form a government.

The meeting quickly followed on the heels of Keir Starmer offering his resignation.

Burnham secured nominations from 379 of the 403 Labour lawmakers in the House of Commons to officially became leader of the Labour Party last week.

Britain's parliamentary democracy allows governing parties to change leaders, and thus prime ministers, without the need for a general election. The next national election doesn't have to be held until 2029.

In his first speech as prime minister, Burnham said he hoped to be a "circuit breaker" to end the trend of instability in British politics.

"Britain ⁠needs to show the world that we ‌can regain our stability once again," Burnham said outside ⁠10 Downing Street.

"We have ⁠not been good ⁠enough, ⁠and ​we need to be ​better."

In ​a clip recorded before he was officially appointed as British ​leader but released after his ⁠speech in ⁠Downing Street, Burnham ‌said that among his first telephone calls internationally would be U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"President Zelenskyy will be ⁠left ⁠in ​no doubt whatsoever that Britain's support is steadfast, ​it is ⁠resolute. It will be there for him, and I will be there for him personally, too," Burnham told reporters.

Can the 'King of the North' fix a fractured Britain?

Zelenskyy was among a number of world leaders to offer congratulations to Burnham on social media, a list that included Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"I look forward to working with Prime Minister Burnham to build greater security, stability and prosperity on both sides of the Atlantic," said Carney.

With respect to Washington, Burnham's predecessor ingratiated himself with Trump for more than a year, only for the U.S. president to later express frustration over what he perceived as Starmer's lack of support for the Iran war. When Starmer announced his plans to resign weeks ago, Trump described him as a "lovely man" and a "sort of friend of mine."

While Burnham has been regarded as one of the Labour Party's best communicators, he faces many of the same problems as his predecessor, including a sluggish economy, a cost-of-living squeeze fuelled by wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and overstretched public services.

Promising Britons "some ⁠breathing space now," he said on Monday that the government would set out some measures to tackle ‌the high cost of living, and how it plans to fund them.

While wishing Burnham "every success," Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch of the Conservative Party touched on the hard choices the new prime minister faced, in a social media post.

How Andy Burnham went from Manchester mayor to U.K. PM

"Every announcement he makes should be properly funded," she said. "We cannot borrow more money and the tax burden is already too high, so the only answer is spending cuts."

Burnham was born in Liverpool, where his father worked as a telephone engineer and his mother as a receptionist. He graduated in English from Cambridge, where he met his wife — Marie-France van Heel, a Dutch-born, Belgian-raised marketing professional known to friends as "Frankie." The couple have three children.

He is not a stranger to federal politics, having first served as MP beginning in 2001 when Tony Blair was prime minister, and later as culture and then health minister under Blair's successor, Gordon Brown.

Burnham mounted unsuccessful bids for the Labour leadership in 2010 and 2015.

Labour regularly trails behind anti-immigration party Reform UK in opinion polls, with an election due no later than 2029. Labour suffered disastrous results in local elections in May, triggering pressure on Starmer to step down that he couldn't resist.

Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage called for an immediate election.

"Andy Burnham cannot be allowed to make the 'biggest changes in politics for 40 years' without a mandate," he said.

Starmer made his farewell speech outside 10 Downing Street before meeting with the king to tender his resignation. He told supporters that "my work is done" and that he was leaving with "good grace" and a "smile."

"I wish him every success," he said of Burnham.

Starmer led Labour a mid-2024 election rout as the party more than doubled its seats from a loss five years earlier, even as its share of the total vote only went up by about two percentage points. Starmer's two years in office marred by missteps and judgment errors that eroded his standing with his party and the public.

Starmer is staying on as MP of Holborn and St. Pancras.

items.title: Spouses of people with dementia have higher risk themselves, study finds
items.summary: Having a spouse with dementia puts you at a higher risk of developing the condition, a new study finds. The researchers suggest the association may be the result of several factors, including what is known as assortative mating.

The researchers suggest the association may be the result of several factors, including what is known as assortative mating. ( ABC News )

About 1 million people were studied to examine dementia risk among married couples.

Researchers found dementia risk was lower among couples with a higher income and more children.

Researchers say couples' lifestyles need to be studied more closely so they can understand diet, exercise and social engagement.

Spouses of people with dementia have a higher risk of developing the condition, but the level of risk can vary depending on income and how many children the couple has, a new study has found.

Research published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) today studied almost 1 million people in Taiwan to examine dementia risk among married couples and what factors might alter that risk.

The researchers found female spouses had a 74 per cent higher risk of all types of dementia if their partner had it, while male spouses had a 69 per cent increased risk if their partner had the condition.

Similar associations were found when researchers studied Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia separately.

The reasons for these associations, the researchers said, may come down to three overlapping factors:

About 1 million people were studied to examine the dementia risk among married couples. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito )

Previous research has established spouses who are primary caregivers often have worse mental health and may develop dementia more often, but co-author of the JAMA study, Chi-Shin Wu, said these past studies had some limitations.

"Many were based on relatively small or regional samples [and] our study included spouses in general and did not assume that every spouse was the primary caregiver," Dr Chi-Shin told the ABC.

"This allowed us to examine dementia risk at the household level rather than attributing the association solely to caregiving."

The researchers used data from Taiwan's National Health Insurance research database, which covers nearly 99 per cent of the population, and identified dementia diagnoses among married individuals between 1998 and 2022.

To make a comparison, they also found married couples where neither had any recorded dementia diagnoses at the same point in time.

They took into account the couple's incomes, the number of children they had, their geographical locations and comorbidities like cardiovascular or mental health.

Simone Reppermund, an expert in cognitive disorders from the Centre for Health Brain Ageing at the University of NSW, who was not involved in the study, said it moved the dial on better understanding the condition.

"The researchers controlled for a lot of factors that are important to control for, which is a real strength of this study, and still the risk of dementia was a lot higher," Dr Reppermund said.

The researchers say spouses should be aware but not alarmed by the findings. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito )

Once the researchers accounted for extra risk, such as age, they found the increased risk corresponded to an additional 2.75 cases of dementia per 100 women and 3.49 cases per 100 men over five years.

The researchers found the risk of dementia was lower for spouses who had more children or a higher income.

Dr Chi-Shin suggested this could be because lower-income households have fewer resources to pay for support, so the spouse has more caregiving stress, while those with fewer children had less potential family support.

"However, because we did not directly measure caregiving responsibilities, intensity or stress, this interpretation remains suggestive rather than conclusive," he said.

Dr Reppermund said income was also a proxy for how well educated someone was, with higher levels of education being a known protective factor against dementia.

But she said people should not assume that having more children always equated to a lower dementia risk.

"The present study showed that number of children played a modifying role, but it depends on the quality of the relationship … the children might be overseas or there might be no relationship whatsoever."

The study's authors acknowledged their research had several limitations, including that they could not analyse the spouses' lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise, smoking, social isolation or hearing.

The World Health Organization recently updated its dementia guidelines to establish the modifiable risk factors for the condition, which can be attributed to 45 per cent of dementia cases.

The risk factors include hearing loss, air pollution, obesity, vision impairment and poor sleep.

Source: World Health Organization

Dr Reppermund said future research must dig deeper into what life looks like for couples where one person has dementia.

"We need to work out whether it's lifestyle that has more of an impact than caregiver stress," she said.

Dr Chi-Shin said spouses should be aware but not alarmed by the research.

"An increased risk is not a certainty, and our observational study does not show that caring for a partner causes dementia. Spouses should not feel blamed for caregiving or assume that they will inevitably develop dementia," he said.

Dr Chi-Shin said spouses must not overlook their own health and continue to look after their sleep, mood, social connections and cardiovascular conditions such as hypertension and diabetes.

They should also access respite care when possible so they can recharge, he added.

At a policy level, Dr Chi-Shin said dementia care must focus more on supporting the household, not just the diagnosed individual.

If this story has prompted any questions or concerns, please call the National Dementia Helpline 1800 100 500 (24 hours, 7 days a week) or visit dementia.org.au.

The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia effective immediately, targeting ships carrying Saudi exports through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthis claim they are acting in response to Saudi Arabia's "oppressive siege" on Yemen over the past 12 years.

The move could put even greater pressure on international energy supplies.

The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, in a move which could put even greater pressure on international energy supplies.

In a statement, the Houthis military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group would enforce the blockade against its "criminal Saudi enemy" effective immediately.

He said the Houthis were acting in response to Saudi Arabia's "oppressive siege" on Yemen over the past 12 years, and promised the rebels would respond to "any foolish act" by their neighbour to break the restrictions with force.

The war between the US, Israel and Iran sent shockwaves through energy markets given the decision by Tehran to block the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies flowed.

About a fifth of the world's oil supplies flowed through the Strait of Hormuz before Tehran blocked the passage when the war broke out. ( Reuters )

While smaller Gulf states such as Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar suffered major disruption to their exports as a result, Saudi Arabia had been able to use its geography to its advantage and pump oil from its large port precincts on the Persian Gulf to facilities on the west coast.

That allowed it to send shipments out through the Red Sea instead — providing a vital lifeline for the Saudi economy and relieving some, but not all, of the pressure on global oil supplies.

The East-West pipeline, as it is known, had come under attack by Iran at the height of the war.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is located between Yemen and Djibouti on the Horn of Africa. ( Getty Images: Gallo )

The new blockade announced by the Houthis suggested the group would target ships carrying Saudi exports transiting through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow waterway between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, acting as the gateway to the Red Sea.

It is not clear whether it will cause further disruption to shipping in the area, given the Red Sea also feeds into the Suez Canal.

Yahya Saree's post about the maritime blockade on X. ( X: Yahya Saree )

The Houthis have previously attacked ships transiting through in protest over the Israel-Gaza war — a move which forced global shipping companies to take massive detours to avoid the area.

The Houthis and the Saudis have been in conflict for more than a decade, as civil war ripped Yemen apart and the Saudis formed a coalition to try to restore the Yemeni government's rule.

A truce brokered in 2022 had largely held until last week, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Yemen's main international airport in a bid to prevent an Iranian plane landing there.

In response, the rebels fired missiles at the Kingdom.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps had threatened to use the Houthis to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as fighting between the US and Iran intensified last week.

Mon 20 Jul 2026 at 10:44pm

Mon 20 Jul 2026 at 10:44pm

Smoke rises from an explosion at an unknown location during what US Central Command says are strikes on Iran. ( US Central Command via Reuters )

The Pentagon identified 1st Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, as the two US soldiers killed while defending against Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan.

The military is examining unidentified remains recovered from the attack site as it searches for a third missing service member.

Iran and the US exchanged fresh strikes across the Middle East, with attacks targeting military assets, commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure, including desalination plants.

The United States has identified two soldiers killed while defending against Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan , as the American military death toll in the war with Iran climbs to 17.

The Pentagon said 1st Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Texas, were killed while supporting the US-led mission against Islamic State in Jordan.

The US warns its citizens to stay away from air and sea ports at Aqaba in southern Jordan, hours before Israeli authorities announced that Iranian missiles had been launched towards the city.

US Central Command said the pair died on Friday while defending against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks. It has not disclosed how they were killed.

A third service member remains missing after the attack, with Central Command saying "unidentified remains" had been recovered from the site and were undergoing examination.

The latest deaths underscore the widening reach of the conflict , with US forces stationed across the Middle East increasingly exposed to Iranian retaliation despite not fighting on the ground inside Iran.

President Donald Trump has defended the military campaign as necessary to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, saying the latest US strikes were carried out "in honour" of the fallen troops.

The conflict began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched strikes targeting Iran's nuclear and missile programs and allied militia groups.

People stand on a bridge destroyed after a strike in Hormozgan province, southern Iran. ( AP Photo: Iranian Students' News Agency )

The first American fatalities came days after the war began, when an Iranian drone strike on a civilian port in Kuwait killed six US soldiers from an Iowa-based logistics unit.

A seventh soldier later died from injuries sustained during an Iranian missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.

In March, six service members were killed when a KC-135 refuelling aircraft supporting operations against Iran crashed in Iraq.

On Saturday, another US service member was killed in northern Iraq while carrying out a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian drone. A second service member was injured.

Separately, the US military said a Navy pilot died after a helicopter crashed into the Arabian Sea earlier this month during what it described as an emergency landing not believed to be caused by hostile action.

The Muwaffaq Salti air base, east of Amman, had been targeted, according to unverified video on social media. ( Supplied: Planet Labs PBC )

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Monday they had launched fresh attacks on US military assets across the Middle East after another night of American air strikes on Iranian cities.

The Guards said they targeted Jordan's Aqaba airport, military facilities in Kuwait and positions in Syria with ballistic missiles.

Sirens sounded in Bahrain, while Kuwait's military said it intercepted hostile drones during the attacks.

Iran also claimed two oil tankers had exploded while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, though Reuters could not independently verify the claim. Separately, British maritime authorities said a commercial vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile off the coast of Oman.

The US warns its citizens to stay away from air and sea ports at Aqaba in southern Jordan, hours before Israeli authorities announced that Iranian missiles had been launched towards the city.

US Central Command said it had conducted a ninth consecutive night of strikes aimed at degrading Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping through the strategic waterway.

The conflict has also expanded to attacks on civilian infrastructure.

Kuwait said one of its desalination plants had been struck for a second consecutive day, causing a fire. Desalination facilities provide most of the drinking water for Gulf nations, raising concerns about water security across the region.

Iran has accused the United States of previously striking one of its own desalination plants and has threatened to retaliate against similar facilities elsewhere in the Gulf.

Iranian authorities say at least 50 people have been killed and more than 500 wounded in US strikes over the past three weeks, while the broader conflict has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon.

Despite the escalating violence, both Washington and Tehran indicated they remained open to renewed negotiations.

Gulf countries and oil companies have been finding ways to bypass the choke point.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States would continue targeting Iran while it threatened international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, but said Washington remained open to a diplomatic solution.

Iran's Foreign Ministry also said diplomacy remained "a tool through which we pursue our national interests, just like war", signalling talks had not been ruled out.

The renewed fighting has also pushed oil prices above US$90 a barrel and driven US petrol prices above US$4 a gallon, adding to political pressure on Mr Trump ahead of November's congressional midterm elections.

scraped.title: Dr. Jill Lepore on the ‘Artificial State’
scraped.description: Harvard law and history professor and New Yorker writer Dr. Jill Lepore discusses her forthcoming book, ‘The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State’
scraped.author: Nilay Patel
scraped.h1: Dr. Jill Lepore on why AI backlash is vital for the future
scraped.body_text:

The Artificial State author explains how counting everything breaks society — and how college grads booing AI might save us all.
